summary: This NASA image article describes a Mastcam photo from NASA's Curiosity Mars Rover showing an evenly layered rock at the edge of "Hidden Valley." The rock is a thick-laminated, evenly stratified deposit interpreted as lake-floor sediment, possibly part of or in front of a delta, where river sediment settled out of the water. It lies beneath cross-bedded sandstones regarded as ancient river deposits. The page credits JPL, Caltech, and Malin Space Science Systems and links to a related Curiosity water-clues article.
one_line: NASA's Curiosity rover imaged evenly layered Martian rock at Hidden Valley, interpreted as an ancient lake-floor sediment deposit near a delta.
key_facts: The image was taken by the Mast Camera (Mastcam) on NASA's Curiosity Mars Rover.
The scene combines multiple frames taken with Mastcam's right-eye camera on Aug. 7, 2014.
The Aug. 7, 2014 observation occurred during the 712th Martian day, or sol, of Curiosity's work on Mars.
The image shows an outcrop at the edge of "Hidden Valley," seen from the valley floor.
The view spans about 5 feet (1.5 meters) across in the foreground.
Figure A includes a superimposed scale bar of 50 centimeters (about 20 inches).
The rock is a thick-laminated, evenly-stratified rock type.
The layered rock forms stratigraphically beneath cross-bedded sandstones regarded as ancient river deposits.
The rocks are interpreted to record sedimentation in a lake, as part of or in front of a delta.
River sediment plumes settled out of the water column and onto the lake floor, according to the interpretation.
NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, a division of the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena, manages the Mars Science Laboratory Project.
JPL designed and built the Curiosity rover.
Malin Space Science Systems, San Diego, built and operates the rover's Mastcam.
The page was last updated Dec 08, 2014, and the responsible NASA official is Abigail Bowman.
